section_summaries.epidemiology: Talaromycosis, caused by the dimorphic fungus Talaromyces marneffei, primarily affects immunocompromised individuals residing in or traveling to the highlands of Southeast Asia, southern China, and northeastern India. HIV-infected individuals with peripheral blood CD4+ T-cell counts ""<=100 cells/µL and those with impaired cellular immunity are at high risk. Although incidence has decreased in Thailand and Hong Kong with high ART coverage, it remains a public health problem in Vietnam and China, accounting for 5% to 15% of annual AIDS admissions and being a leading cause of HIV-associated bloodstream infection. Cases diagnosed outside endemic areas are increasing due to migration and international travel. It also emerges as an opportunistic infection in individuals with adult-onset primary immunodeficiency (anti-interferon-gamma auto-antibodies) or secondary immunodeficiency (autoimmune diseases, malignancies, transplantations requiring immunosuppression). T. marneffei has been isolated from the lungs, liver, and spleen of bamboo rats (Rhizomys spp. and Cannomys badius), soil samples, and bamboo rat feces near burrows. Exposure to animals, plants, and travel to highlands are risk factors, suggesting soil in highland regions as a natural reservoir. Epidemiologic data support soil as a reservoir, with a 30-50% increase in incidence during the rainy season and humid months, indicating interaction with multiple reservoirs in expanding its biomass and geography.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: The mechanisms by which T. marneffei invades the host are not well understood, but infection is presumed to occur via inhalation of environmental conidia. Macrophages are the primary line of host defense, phagocytizing conidia through an L-arginine-dependent nitric oxide pathway. CD4+ T-cell-mediated immunity, producing Th1 cytokines like interleukin-12, gamma interferon, and tumor necrosis factor alpha, is essential for infection control. Healthy individuals can control the pathogen post-acquisition, though quiescent infection can persist and reactivate later. Failure of both innate and cellular immune responses leads to pathogen invasion and dissemination through the reticuloendothelial system. The fungal cell wall's highly antigenic mannoprotein, T. marneffei Mp1p, enhances survival within macrophages and acts as a critical virulence factor in a mouse model by binding and sequestering arachidonic acids, a key proinflammatory lipid, to dampen host innate immune response.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: Disseminated infection involving multiple organ systems is the most common manifestation, particularly in profoundly immunosuppressed HIV-infected patients with CD4+ T-cell counts ">=100 cells/mm³." Patients often present with fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and respiratory and gastrointestinal abnormalities, which are non-specific and can be indistinguishable from disseminated tuberculosis. Characteristic central-necrotic papules develop in 60-70% of patients on the face, neck, chest, back, and upper extremities. Common laboratory findings include anemia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated serum aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase. Primary central nervous system infections have been reported. Localized infections are more common in non-HIV-infected patients, including chronic pulmonary cavity lesions, abdominal abscesses, obstructive tracheal lesions, genital chancroid, pericardial effusion, and osteoarthritis. Untreated disseminated infection is fatal, with an on-treatment mortality of up to 30%, higher with delayed diagnosis, older age, shorter duration of symptoms, dyspnea, absence of fever or skin lesions, thrombocytopenia, and elevated lactate dehydrogenase levels. Profoundly immunosuppressed patients initiating ART are at risk for Talaromycosis Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS), presenting as paradoxical worsening or unmasking of infection. IRIS manifestations include exacerbated skin lesions (erythematous nodules, verrucous lesions, inflammatory plaques), fever, lymphadenopathy, aseptic arthritis of large and small joints, or erythema nodosum. Co-infection with microbiologically confirmed tuberculosis occurs in 22% of patients, complicating management, and cryptococcal meningitis is a rare but challenging co-infection.
section_summaries.diagnosis: A presumptive diagnosis of talaromycosis can be made by microscopic examination of Giemsa- or Wright-stained smears from skin lesions, lymph nodes, or bone marrow aspirates, revealing oval-to-round intra-macrophage and extra-macrophage yeasts with characteristic central septa. The definitive diagnosis is based on culture isolation of the pathogen, demonstrating temperature-dependent dimorphic growth; however, this can take up to 2 weeks for identification, contributing to delayed diagnosis and higher mortality. PCR-based assays have been developed to improve diagnostic accuracy and speed, showing high specificity but low sensitivity (60-70%) due to low circulating fungal DNA and difficulties in releasing DNA from the fungal cell wall. Monoclonal antibody-based antigen detection assays have demonstrated higher sensitivities than blood culture and PCR, with the Mp1p-based antigen detection assay showing 90% sensitivity and 98% specificity, currently under commercial development.
section_summaries.treatment: International guidelines recommend initial therapy with amphotericin B deoxycholate for 2 weeks, followed by itraconazole consolidation therapy for 10 weeks, and maintenance therapy until CD4 counts are ">100 cells/mm³" for at least 6 months. A multicenter trial confirmed amphotericin B's superiority to itraconazole for initial therapy in terms of 6-month mortality, IRIS, and relapse incidence. Fungal clearance data suggest a shorter course of amphotericin (<=8 days) might be effective, but requires further study. Liposomal amphotericin B and voriconazole are also effective, though often unavailable in resource-limited settings. For Talaromycosis IRIS, continuing ART, antifungal therapy, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medications, and judicious use of corticosteroids for joint involvement are recommended. Co-infection with tuberculosis requires therapeutic drug monitoring (if available) and increased itraconazole doses due to interactions with rifampicin. Co-infection with cryptococcal meningitis may require new triazole drugs effective against both pathogens, such as voriconazole or isavuconazole, as itraconazole or fluconazole alone are not effective for maintenance.
section_summaries.prevention: Primary prophylaxis with itraconazole has been shown to prevent invasive fungal infections in patients with CD4 counts "<200 cells/mm³" in Thailand. However, this strategy has not been widely adopted in Asia due to high costs, concerns of toxicity, and the potential for drug resistance.
